meta.title: Who really said "No great thing is created suddenly, any more than a bunch of grapes or a fig. If you tell me that you desire a fig, I answer you that there must be time. Let it first blossom, then bear fruit, then ripen"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Epictetus really said it — Discourses I.15.7, recorded by Arrian. The famous English wording comes from T. W. Higginson's 1865 revision of Elizabeth Carter.

answer.sourceLine: Genuine. The passage stands at Discourses I.15.7, in the chapter “What Philosophy Promises,” taken down by his pupil Arrian. This exact English, however, is a translator’s: it first appears in Thomas Wentworth Higginson’s revision of Elizabeth Carter’s translation ↗, first published Boston: Little, Brown, 1865 — the scan linked here is the 1866 printing, same text, p. 48.

source.heading: The source

source.excerpt: But the inquirer still further asking for a rule for self-government, if he should not be reconciled; Epictetus answered thus: — No great thing is created suddenly; any more than a bunch of grapes or a fig. If you tell me, that you desire a fig, I answer you, that there must be time. Let it first blossom, then bear fruit, then ripen. Since then, the fruit of a fig-tree is not brought to perfection suddenly, or in one hour; do you think to possess instantaneously and easily the fruit of the human mind? I warn you, expect it not.
trail: Epictetus wrote nothing himself. His pupil Arrian compiled the Discourses around AD 108 ↗; of the original eight books, four survive.

The passage sits at Discourses I.15.7, in the chapter “What Philosophy Promises.” Wikiquote’s sourced Book I section ↗ carries the Greek and a near-identical English rendering under that citation — its text reads “No thing great is created suddenly…” and names no translator.

Elizabeth Carter’s eighteenth-century opening sentence is noticeably different — the 1759 Dublin printing ↗ reads “No great Thing is brought to Perfection suddenly; when not so much as a Bunch of Grapes or a Fig is.” Her closing, though, is the familiar one: “Let it first blossom, then bear Fruit, then ripen” (p. 45).
The familiar wording appears in Higginson’s 1866 revision of Carter ↗ at Book I, ch. XV, p. 48, and again in the 1890 revised edition.
source.excerptNote: The 1866 printing puts a semicolon after “suddenly” and a comma after “If you tell me.” The revised edition (New York: Thomas Nelson and Sons, 1890, pp. 55–56) prints “No great thing is created suddenly, any more than a bunch of grapes or a fig. If you tell me that you desire a fig…” — nearly the punctuation that circulates today, though both printings still keep a comma after “I answer you.” The closing sentences about the fig-tree are almost always dropped in quotation.

author.name: Epictetus
author.heading: About Epictetus
author.metaLine: c. AD 50 – c. 135 · Greek Stoic philosopher, born enslaved
author.bio: Epictetus was born into slavery at Hierapolis in Phrygia and served the freedman Epaphroditus in Rome before gaining his freedom after Nero’s death. When Domitian banished philosophers from the city he opened a school at Nicopolis in Greece, teaching that we control our judgements and nothing else. He wrote nothing himself: everything we have comes from his student Arrian, who said he wrote the lectures down as nearly word for word as he could.

misattribution.heading: The part that gets lost
misattribution.intro: The name on this quote is right: Epictetus really is behind it. What gets dropped is the translator — and translators disagree sharply about how to render the line.

items.why: Epictetus taught in Koine Greek and left no writings; Arrian took the lectures down ↗. The polished opening sentence people share is Thomas Wentworth Higginson’s, first printed in 1865; the closing “Let it first blossom…” he kept from Elizabeth Carter.

items.scope: Partly her wording, kept by Higginson —
items.why: Only the opening sentence is Higginson’s rewrite: Carter’s own text ↗ reads “No great Thing is brought to Perfection suddenly; when not so much as a Bunch of Grapes or a Fig is.” The famous closing — “Let it first blossom, then bear Fruit, then ripen” — is Carter word for word (1759 Dublin printing, p. 45), and Higginson only lightly trimmed the sentence between.

items.scope: The wording, credited to the common Victorian version
items.why: Long’s translation ↗ renders it “Nothing great, said Epictetus, is produced suddenly, since not even the grape or the fig is” — a different sentence entirely.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Epictetus’ and the citation is solid — Discourses I.15.7. The memorable English comes from Higginson’s revision of Carter ↗: the opening sentence is his, the closing line is hers, and the credit belongs to both.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Someone came to Epictetus with a very ordinary complaint: my brother treats me badly, how do I make him stop? Epictetus refused the premise. Philosophy, he said, does not procure outward goods; the material of the art of living is your own life, not your brother’s. When the man pressed — fine, but how do I keep myself steady if he never comes round? — the fig answer is what he got.

It is a deliberately unglamorous image. Not an oak, not a mountain: a fig, the most everyday fruit on a Greek table. The point is that character ripens on the same schedule as produce, and the closing lines that almost never get quoted make it sting — if a fig tree cannot be hurried, why would you expect the fruit of a human mind in an hour?
context.detailsSummary: More about Epictetus and the Discourses
detailsBody: Epictetus was born enslaved at Hierapolis in Phrygia and freed after Nero’s death; when Domitian expelled philosophers from Rome he set up a school at Nicopolis in north-western Greece, and it is those classroom sessions Arrian preserved.
Four of the original eight books of the Discourses survive. The fig passage closes Book I, chapter 15 — one of the shortest chapters in the collection.
